title: Rate limiter requirements
idea: Scoping a rate limiter means deciding who is counted, how many requests each key gets per time window, what a rejected caller hears, and what v1 leaves out.
points: A rule names a key type, a limit, and a time window.
Every call returns a decision: allowed, or rejected with a retry-after hint.
Each key has its own budget, so one noisy caller cannot starve others.
Assume many keys and a fast check; the limiter sits on every request.

hero.title: Actors and use cases in v1

edges.caption: Every incoming request asks the limiter one question: may this key go ahead now?
The answer carries how many calls remain, or how long to wait before trying again.
An operator sets the rules, for example 100 requests per 60 seconds per API key.

edges.label: used by
edges.caption: The check reads the rule that matches the caller's key type.
Time is an actor too: as it passes, spent budget returns to each key.

edges.label: feeds
edges.caption: The check uses the refilled budget, so a rejected key can succeed later.
A limit shared across servers, billing quotas and network floods wait for later. Say so out loud.

code.title: Rules and scope as code
code.caption: The rules are data with an invariant, and the v1 scope is an enum you can read aloud.

walk.text: Three `LimitRule`s: each picks a key type, a limit and a window in seconds.
List every use case with its actor and an IN or OUT tag.
A rule with a zero limit or window can never be built.
Four use cases form v1: check, report, configure, refill.
Three are named and cut, so the boundary is visible in the design.

pitfalls: Ask which key is counted before choosing an algorithm; it changes everything.
Agree what a rejection returns: status, remaining count, and when to retry.
Say whether one server or a fleet shares the limit; v1 here is one process.

quiz.q: An interviewer says only "design a rate limiter". What do you settle first?
options: How to store counters in a database
Which HTTP framework will host it
The key, the rate, and what a rejection returns
quiz.why: The key, the rate and the rejection contract define the interface. Algorithm, storage and framework are choices made to serve them.

takeaway: Fix the key, the rate, and the rejection contract before any algorithm.

starters: Should I limit by API key, user id, or IP address?
What should happen when the limiter itself fails?
How do burst limits differ from average rate limits?
